questions.question: Q: Name five modes of fossil preservation.

points.text: 1) Original material (amber, permafrost). 2) Replacement (original mineral replaced atom by atom). 3) Permineralisation (minerals fill pores). 4) Mould and cast. 5) Compression (carbon film).

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between a body fossil and a trace fossil?

points.text: A body fossil preserves part of the organism itself (shell, bone, leaf). A trace fossil preserves evidence of the organism's activity (footprint, burrow, coprolite) but not the body.

questions.question: Q: How can fossils indicate past environments?

points.text: Living organisms have specific environmental requirements. Finding their fossils indicates those conditions existed: coral fossils indicate warm shallow marine conditions; coal-forming plants indicate humid swamps; dropstones indicate glacial conditions.

questions.question: Q: Why is the fossil record incomplete?

points.text: Most organisms decompose rapidly after death. Fossilisation requires rapid burial in sediment, which is uncommon. Soft-bodied organisms rarely fossilise. Even fossilised remains can be destroyed by erosion, metamorphism or melting.

questions.question: Q: What conditions favour fossil preservation?

points.text: Rapid burial in fine sediment (prevents decay and scavenging), anoxic conditions (limits decomposition), hard body parts (shells, bones fossilise more easily than soft tissue), and absence of destructive geological processes.
